title: W.W.W. Associates, Inc. v. Giancontieri
summary: New York enforced a written cancellation right given to either party and refused outside evidence offered to turn it into a right benefiting only the buyer.

sections.Parties: The buyer, W.W.W. Associates, sought specific performance of a land-sale contract. The sellers relied on the written right to cancel because litigation affecting the property remained unresolved.
sections.Material Facts:
The agreement contemplated a December 1986 closing. A clause postponed closing during pending litigation concerning the property and allowed either party to cancel if the litigation had not concluded by June 1, 1987. The buyer said this clause was added solely to protect its ability to obtain financing and title insurance for a planned senior-housing project.

By late May the buyer was willing to close despite the litigation. On June 2 the sellers canceled and returned the deposit. The buyer alleged that the sellers had stopped defending the litigation while waiting to escape the sale and seek a higher price. The sellers did not contest those assertions for purposes of their motion; they relied on the written language.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court granted summary judgment to the sellers. The Appellate Division reversed and directed specific performance for the buyer based on its account of the clause’s purpose. The New York Court of Appeals reversed and dismissed the complaint.
sections.Issue: Could outside evidence that a reciprocal cancellation clause was intended solely for the buyer’s benefit prevent enforcement of its unambiguous terms?
sections.Holding: No. The court would not use extrinsic evidence to create ambiguity in a complete agreement clear on its face.
sections.Reasoning:
The buyer’s waiver theory required establishing that the condition existed for its sole benefit. The written agreement, however, expressly gave the right to either party. The court treated the buyer’s account of negotiations as legally immaterial to that unambiguous allocation.

The opinion emphasizes commercial certainty, especially for real property. Enforcing clear writings reduces the risks of unreliable memory, fraudulent later assertions, and unpredictable resolution by juries. The judge first determines ambiguity as a matter of law from the agreement, rather than beginning with testimony that assigns different rights.

The sellers’ failure to dispute the buyer’s factual narrative did not make that narrative dispositive. A factual dispute matters only if the governing substantive rule makes the fact relevant. This is the course’s central contrast with Pacific Gas: courts disagree about what evidence can be considered at the initial ambiguity stage.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It explains why strong evidence about negotiations may fail to affect a result under a rule that gives a clear writing controlling force.

topics.interpretation: New York refused to create ambiguity through external negotiation evidence.
topics.assent: The final written allocation controlled over the buyer’s account of intended benefit.
topics.conditions: The agreement expressly allocated a cancellation right after unresolved litigation.
topics.governing-law: The decision contrasts with California’s contextual approach.

mnemonic.rationale: A cancellation clause read as written
